extracted.intended_audience: users of the Metamath Proof Explorer / contributors to set.mm; mathematicians and students learning formal proof development with Metamath
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and technical standards for expressing, proving, and organizing Metamath assertions (theorems, deductions, axioms) in the set.mm database, including syntax conventions, proof style (deduction/ND), and the axioms used for real and complex numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading $e (ϕ → ∀x ϕ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis of the form $e (ϕ → ∀ x ϕ) should be read “assume variable x is (effectively) not free in wff ϕ.” Literally: assume it is provable that ϕ → ∀x ϕ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This syntactic device avoids complexities associated with the standard treatment of free and bound variables. Use it when you want to state that x is effectively not free in ϕ without explicit variable-occurrence checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using antecedent ¬ ∀ x x = y → ... to mean distinct variables
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of the forms a ... (¬ ∀ x x = y → ...) or p ... (¬ ∀ x x = y → ...) should be read “if x and y are distinct variables, then...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This antecedent is a technical device to avoid needing the $d statement early; it permits simpler symbol manipulations analogous to propositional calculus. Remember the $d statement eventually becomes required.

rubrics_metrics.name: $d x y
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement $d x y should be read “assume x and y are distinct variables.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use $d statements to assert distinct-variable restrictions explicitly when needed in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: $d x ϕ
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement $d x ϕ should be read “assume x does not occur in ϕ.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to assert absence of a variable from a wff; can be used instead of more verbose syntactic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: $d x A
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement $d x A should be read “assume variable x does not occur in class A.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for class-variable occurrence restrictions; common in meta-level bookkeeping of Metamath assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit substitution via restriction+hypothesis group
rubrics_metrics.description: The restriction and hypothesis group $d x A; $d x ψ; $e ( x = A → ( ϕ ↔ ψ ) ) is used to mean “assume ψ results from the proper substitution of A for x in ϕ.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit substitution is a style choice that can shorten proofs compared to explicit substitution. Sometimes $e (ψ → ∀x ψ) is used instead of $d x ψ when only effective non-freeness is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: $e A ∈ V
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis $e A ∈ V should be read “assume class A is a set (i.e., exists).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a convenient Quine-style convention in set.mm to indicate existence/membership in the universe V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction/hypothesis for effective non-freeness in classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The restriction and hypothesis $d x y; $e ( y ∈ A → ∀ x y ∈ A ) should be read “assume variable x is (effectively) not free in class A.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this technical device when handling membership statements involving classes where explicit variable freeness is cumbersome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceability of Metamath proofs to axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath proofs allow you to trace the derivation of any theorem back to axioms (the set.mm database supports traceability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transparency is a key advantage: proofs are constructed from substitution and listed axioms/theorems, and tools (e.g., show trace_back) let you inspect derivations to their foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution as the single fundamental proof rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Every step in every Metamath proof uses only the single substitution rule (one substitution rule is sufficient to express all rules of logic and axioms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mastering substitution lets you apply every Metamath proof technique. Structure proofs as sequences of substitutions justified by previously proved theorems/definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof step format and justifications (Step / Expression / Ref / Hyp)
rubrics_metrics.description: In proof displays each 'Step' is a sequential number, 'Expression' is the proved expression, 'Ref' is the theorem or axiom justifying it, and 'Hyp' lists previous steps that satisfy needed hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each proof step cites a reference and any hypotheses it depends on; in HTML output references are clickable for inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath theorem labelling and omission of $d/$f in summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: For brevity the chapter omits the $d restrictions or $f hypotheses when listing theorems; consult the set.mm database if uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a listed theorem in practice, check its full declaration in set.mm for any missing $d/$f or other hypotheses you must satisfy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-resscn (R ⊆ C)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. The real numbers are a subset of the complex numbers. ax-resscn $p ( R ⊆ C )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the 22 axioms assumed for R and C in set.mm; treat these as the starting algebraic/order axioms for analysis within set.mm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-1cn (1 ∈ C)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2. One is a complex number. ax-1cn $p ( 1 ∈ C )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 1 as a given element of the complex numbers in constructions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-icn (i ∈ C)
rubrics_metrics.description: 3. The imaginary number i is a complex number. ax-icn $p ( i ∈ C )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include i in C when reasoning about complex-specific properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-addcl (closure under addition in C)
rubrics_metrics.description: 4. Complex numbers are closed under addition. ax-addcl $p ( ( A ∈ C ∧ B ∈ C ) → ( A + B ) ∈ C )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when proving closure properties or forming sums within C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-addrcl (closure under addition in R)
rubrics_metrics.description: 5. Real numbers are closed under addition. ax-addrcl $p ( ( A ∈ R ∧ B ∈ R ) → ( A + B ) ∈ R )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when manipulating sums of real elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-mulcl (closure under multiplication in C)
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. Complex numbers are closed under multiplication. ax-mulcl $p ( ( A ∈ C ∧ B ∈ C ) → ( A · B ) ∈ C )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for product formation within C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-mulrcl (closure under multiplication in R)
rubrics_metrics.description: 7. Real numbers are closed under multiplication. ax-mulrcl $p ( ( A ∈ R ∧ B ∈ R ) → ( A · B ) ∈ R )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when reasoning about products of real numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-mulcom (commutativity of multiplication in C)
rubrics_metrics.description: 8. Multiplication of complex numbers is commutative. ax-mulcom $p ( ( A ∈ C ∧ B ∈ C ) → ( A · B ) = ( B · A ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for algebraic rearrangements; note independence of this axiom is unresolved in context of the other axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-addass (associativity of addition in C)
rubrics_metrics.description: 9. Addition of complex numbers is associative. ax-addass $p ( ( A ∈ C ∧ B ∈ C ∧ C ∈ C ) → ( ( A + B ) + C ) = ( A + ( B + C ) ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to re-associate sums in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-mulass (associativity of multiplication in C)
rubrics_metrics.description: 10. Multiplication of complex numbers is associative. ax-mulass $p ( ( A ∈ C ∧ B ∈ C ∧ C ∈ C ) → ( ( A · B ) · C ) = ( A · ( B · C ) ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to regroup products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-distr (distributivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: 11. Multiplication distributes over addition for complex numbers. ax-distr $p ( ( A ∈ C ∧ B ∈ C ∧ C ∈ C ) → ( A · ( B + C ) ) = ( ( A · B ) + ( A · C ) ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential for algebraic expansion and manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-i2m1 (i^2 + 1 = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: 12. The square of i equals −1 (expressed as ( i · i ) + 1 = 0 ). ax-i2m1 $p ( ( i · i ) + 1 ) = 0
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the imaginary unit algebraically; use in complex-specific algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-1ne0 (1 ≠ 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: 13. One and zero are distinct. ax-1ne0 $p ( 1 =/ 0 )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental field-like separation of unit and zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-1rid (1 is multiplicative identity in R)
rubrics_metrics.description: 14. One is an identity element for real multiplication. ax-1rid $p ( A ∈ R → ( A · 1 ) = A )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when simplifying products involving 1 in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-rnegex (existence of additive inverse in R)
rubrics_metrics.description: 15. Every real number has a negative. ax-rnegex $p ( A ∈ R → ∃ x ∈ R ( A + x ) = 0 )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to prove existence of additive inverses in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-rrecex (existence of multiplicative inverse for nonzero reals)
rubrics_metrics.description: 16. Every nonzero real number has a reciprocal. ax-rrecex $p ( A ∈ R → ( A =/ 0 → ∃ x ∈ R ( A · x ) = 1 ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to justify division by nonzero real numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-cnre (complex numbers as two reals)
rubrics_metrics.description: 17. A complex number can be expressed in terms of two reals. ax-cnre $p ( A ∈ C → ∃ x ∈ R ∃ y ∈ R A = ( x + ( y · i ) ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to reduce complex-number statements to pairs of real components when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-pre-lttri (strict trichotomy on R)
rubrics_metrics.description: 18. Ordering on reals satisfies strict trichotomy. ax-pre-lttri $p ( ( A ∈ R ∧ B ∈ R ) → ( A < B ↔ ¬ ( A = B ∨ B < A ) ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in order reasoning on reals to decide comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-pre-lttrn (transitivity of < on R)
rubrics_metrics.description: 19. Ordering on reals is transitive. ax-pre-lttrn $p ( ( A ∈ R ∧ B ∈ R ∧ C ∈ R ) → ( ( A < B ∧ B < C ) → A < C ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard transitivity property for reasoning about inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-pre-ltadd (preservation of order under addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: 20. Ordering on reals is preserved after addition to both sides. ax-pre-ltadd $p ( ( A ∈ R ∧ B ∈ R ∧ C ∈ R ) → ( A < B → ( C + A ) < ( C + B ) ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to translate inequalities when adding the same real to both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-pre-mulgt0 (product of positives > 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: 21. The product of two positive reals is positive. ax-pre-mulgt0 $p ( ( A ∈ R ∧ B ∈ R ) → ( ( 0 < A ∧ 0 < B ) → 0 < ( A · B ) ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply in positivity reasoning and sign analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom ax-pre-sup (completeness / supremum property)
rubrics_metrics.description: 22. A non-empty, bounded-above set of reals has a supremum. ax-pre-sup $p ( ( A ⊆ R ∧ A =/ ∅ ∧ ∃ x ∈ R ∀ y ∈ A y < x ) → ∃ x ∈ R ( ∀ y ∈ A ¬ x < y ∧ ∀ y ∈ R ( y < x → ∃ z ∈ A y < z ) ) )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the completeness axiom for R; use when working with suprema/limits and other completeness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating unnecessary complex-number axioms (minimality/independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Over time some previous complex-number axioms were proven redundant or derivable from others (examples: C ∈ V; commutativity of +; A + 0 = A; existence of additive inverses in C; existence of multiplicative inverses in C for nonzero elements; 0 ∈ R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a minimal axiom set: eliminate or weaken axioms when they can be formally derived. Check formal proofs (and dates/authors) in set.mm for redundancy; be aware that independence of some axioms (e.g., ax-mulcom) may be an open question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of definitions in proofs (example: df-2, df-3, df-4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions such as df-2 (2 = 1 + 1), df-3, df-4 are used directly in steps of a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ definitions early to instantiate arithmetic identities; proofs commonly use definitions as the very first justifications for expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding proof-step dependency (Hyp column)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a referenced theorem requires hypotheses, list previous steps that satisfy those hypotheses in the Hyp column so the reference can be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly show which earlier steps fulfill required hypotheses; this is how substitution instances are validated in stepwise proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard Deduction Theorem (SDT) is algorithmic but impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: The Standard Deduction Theorem provides an algorithm to convert a deduction (ϕ ⇒ ψ) to a theorem (ϕ → ψ) by rewriting each proof step, but applying it directly can cause exponential blowup and has subtle restrictions (e.g., generalization axiom involvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on automatically expanding SDT in practice; instead use Metamath-friendly alternatives. If SDT is invoked informally in reasoning, recognize it's a metatheorem and that explicit expansion would be huge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak Deduction Theorem (dedth) usage and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Weak Deduction Theorem is a more efficient method that produces a theorem from a special substitution instance of a deduction using a small fixed number of steps. It requires proving a special-case theorem of the deduction's hypothesis (e.g., 1 ∈ R) and that certain substitutions/equivalences hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you see a proof referencing dedth, examine the step immediately before it (substituted deduction) and the auxiliary theorem used to fulfill dedth's technical condition. Use dedth when you can establish the required special-case hypothesis as an independent theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction style (prefered method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write assertions in deduction form: preface each non-definition hypothesis and the conclusion with a common antecedent (usually ϕ →). Deduction-form assertions have hypotheses that are implications with the same antecedent or definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer deduction style in set.mm: label deduction-form assertions with a 'd' suffix; it avoids the complexity of SDT and often yields clearer, shorter proofs. Convert to inference or closed form mechanically (use a1i, trud, simpr, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed / Deduction / Inference forms (definitions & conversions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed form: assertion with no hypotheses. Deduction form: assertion with hypotheses and conclusion prefixed by a common antecedent (ϕ →). Inference form: hypotheses not sharing a common antecedent. Conversion: use mechanical steps (a1i to insert T.→, trud to remove) or prove conjunctions of consequents to get closed form from deduction form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the documented mechanical recipes (a1i, trud, simpr, simp* theorems and syl chaining) to move between forms; leverage proven simp* proofs or let the Metamath program minimize steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Deduction in Metamath via deduction form
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural Deduction can be represented in Metamath by writing assertions in deduction form and using MPE assertions that correspond to ND rules (e.g., jca corresponds to ∧-I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To add an ND assumption, add it to the antecedent (e.g., using adantr); to depend on a new assumption, use simpr; to apply assertions outside the ND scope, add the ND antecedent to that assertion. Follow the documented ND-to-MPE translations (see Carneiro's presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended workflow for hypothesis-to-antecedent conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: The recommended approach is: prefer Mario Carneiro’s natural deduction method (deduction form), then use the Weak Deduction Theorem where ND is hard to apply, and use the Standard Deduction Theorem only as a last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ordering avoids adding external metalogic and keeps proofs within the Hilbert-style MPE framework while maintaining manageability and rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware proof-length explosion when expanding basic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Only using very basic natural deduction rules or only axioms can yield very long proofs (same issue as expanding SDT): reuse already-proven assertions in deduction form to keep proofs shorter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reusing higher-level lemmas/theorems and deduction-form assertions to produce clear, succinct proofs rather than reconstructing everything from primitive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice for following proofs that use dedth
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof references dedth (or dedthxx), you can follow the proof easily by clicking the theorem referenced in the step just before the dedth reference and ignoring the technical machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this shortcut to focus on the 'important' conceptual steps of a proof; inspect the technical steps only when you need to reproduce the exact conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath’s Hilbert-style basis with ND equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath Proof Explorer is fundamentally Hilbert-style (many axioms, few inference rules) but can emulate natural deduction by using deduction form and ND-equivalent theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the ND-equivalent MPE assertions for common ND rules to construct proofs that resemble natural deduction while remaining formalizable in the Hilbert-style MPE.
